title: rowfold (example package): where do you stand?
intro: Four short questions about how rowfold, an example package, should trade one good thing against another. Answer from how the project actually behaves, not how you wish it did.

glossary.name: Portability
glossary.definition: The range of Python versions, operating systems, CPU architectures and runtimes on which rowfold installs and gives the same results without extra tools.

glossary.name: Performance
glossary.definition: How quickly, and within how little memory, rowfold reads and transforms large files on a single machine.

glossary.name: Approachability
glossary.definition: How quickly someone new to rowfold gets a correct first result from the documentation, without help.

glossary.name: Correctness
glossary.definition: The degree to which every table rowfold returns matches what the file actually holds, or rowfold raises a clear error instead of returning a guess.

glossary.name: Compatibility
glossary.definition: The degree to which code written against an earlier rowfold release keeps working, unchanged, on the latest one.

glossary.name: Clarity
glossary.definition: How easily a reader can predict what an API call does from its name, arguments and type hints alone.

widgets.prompt: When rowfold could be faster with compiled code, where should it sit between portability and raw speed?
If rowfold can only protect two of these fully, how would you weight all three?

widgets.scenario: The skip argument of read() skips rows, but many users expect it to skip columns. About forty downstream packages pass skip= today.

options.label: Add a clearer skip_rows and deprecate skip
options.detail: skip keeps working with a warning for two minor releases, then goes away in the next major release.

options.label: Keep skip and fix the documentation
options.detail: No downstream code changes; the name stays confusing for new users.

widgets.flip_prompt: What would make you pick the other option?
